source.version: Journal version of record: AI (MDPI) 2025, 6, 247, https://doi.org/10.3390/ai6100247; received 20 July 2025, revised 30 August 2025, accepted 16 September 2025, published 1 October 2025 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Creativeable: Leveraging AI for Personalized Creativity Enhancement

supplement.holds: Text S1 to S4 (prompts for word triplets, for feedback and difficulty adjustment, for GPT-4 story scoring, and the reflection questions) and Tables S1 (word triplets with semantic distance and difficulty ratings) and S2 (examples of improvement suggestions). The listing names no outcome statistics; the main text holds all reported statistics. Data and code are on OSF.

paper_design_summary: 385 Prolific participants completed five rounds of a short story writing task in one of four Creativeable conditions crossing GPT-4 feedback (yes/no) with GPT-4 adaptive task difficulty (varying/constant). Conditions were filled in four separate recruitment batches, one per condition; the paper does not state random assignment. Alternative Uses Task originality (OCSAI automated scoring) and fluency were measured before and after training without AI, and each training story was scored for creativity by GPT-4.

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of four training conditions: feedback with varying difficulty (F/VL), feedback with constant difficulty (F/CL), no feedback with varying difficulty (NF/VL), no feedback with constant difficulty (NF/CL). Each condition was filled by its own recruitment batch.
assignment.quote: Recruitment was conducted in four separate batches, each corresponding to one of the study's experimental conditions, to ensure smooth operation of the study platform.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1; also p. 23, Section 4.5 ("Data collection in separate batches raises potential concerns about temporal differences")

arms.name: F/VL
arms.description: GPT-4 'creativity trainer' gives general feedback and one creativity improvement suggestion after each round and adjusts word-triplet difficulty each round from performance and self-reported fatigue

arms.name: F/CL
arms.description: Same GPT-4 feedback and suggestions as F/VL; task difficulty fixed at medium-easy across five rounds

arms.name: NF/VL
arms.description: No feedback; GPT-4 trainer adjusts task difficulty each round

arms.name: NF/CL
arms.description: Control condition: neither feedback nor difficulty adjustment; difficulty constant

participants.exclusions: Participants were excluded if they did not complete the study, gave overly brief responses, or completed the tasks unusually quickly; the number excluded is not stated. 385 is the count included.
participants.who: Prolific crowd workers, native English speakers aged 18-45 with at least 12 years of formal education, paid 9 GBP per hour
participants.quote: A total of 385 participants were included in the study, recruited via the crowdsourcing platform Prolific.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the OpenAI API (the 'creativity trainer')
ai_tool.how_used: In feedback conditions, after each story the trainer gave two-sentence general feedback on the story and one suggestion for improving creativity or brainstorming in the next round; it supplied no story content. In varying-level conditions it chose whether to raise, keep, or lower the difficulty of the next word triplet. Participants wrote the stories themselves. No AI was available during the pre- and post-training AUT and semantic fluency tasks.

task.description: Training task: five rounds of writing a 60-80 word story that integrates three semantically distant words. Assessment task (outcome): Alternative Uses Task with two items before and two items after training, plus an animal semantic fluency control task.
task.duration: Whole study about 50 minutes on average; 2 minutes per AUT item and 2 minutes for the semantic fluency task (p. 10)

outcomes.name: Post-training AUT originality (OCSAI score)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: OCSAI online platform (prompted GPT instance) scores originality of each use 1-5; averaged within item, then over the two post-training items. Paper analyzes it as a pre/post mixed ANOVA, a one-way ANOVA on post-training scores with Tukey HSD, and percentage improvement from pre to post (same outcome, variant).
outcomes.delay: Measured right after the five training rounds in the same ~50-minute session

contrasts.reported: Post: F/CL M = 2.81 (SD = 0.38) vs NF/CL M = 2.84 (SD = 0.35); pre: 2.56 (SD 0.40) vs 2.63 (SD 0.37); n = 98 vs 97 (Table 1). Improvement rate F/CL M = 11.6%, SD = 17.42%, 95%CI = [8.11, 15.09] vs NF/CL M = 9.42%, SD = 15.0%, 95%CI = [6.41, 12.44]. Paper: other post-training pairwise comparisons and other improvement-rate comparisons not statistically significant.
contrasts.locator: pp. 13-14, Section 3.2.1 and Figure 3; p. 6, Table 1

contrasts.reported: Post: F/VL M = 2.71 (SD = 0.44) vs NF/CL M = 2.84 (SD = 0.35); pre: 2.60 (SD 0.34) vs 2.63 (SD 0.37); n = 97 vs 97. Improvement rate F/VL M = 4.82%, SD = 16.2%, 95%CI = [1.57, 8.09] vs NF/CL 9.42%, SD = 15.0%, 95%CI = [6.41, 12.44]. Pairwise difference reported as not significant.

Post: NF/VL M = 2.89 (SD = 0.41) vs NF/CL M = 2.84 (SD = 0.35); pre: 2.67 (SD 0.33) vs 2.63 (SD 0.37); n = 93 vs 97. Improvement rate NF/VL M = 8.61%, SD = 14.14%, 95%CI = [5.7, 11.52] vs NF/CL 9.42%. Pairwise difference reported as not significant. In NF/VL the AI only sets task difficulty.

Post-training one-way ANOVA F(3, 381) = 3.34, p = 0.002, eta2 = 0.025; Tukey HSD NF/VL vs F/VL: deltaM = 0.175, SE = 0.06, p = 0.014, Cohen's d = 0.41. Post means F/VL 2.71 (SD 0.44) vs NF/VL 2.89 (SD 0.41).

Improvement rate (pre to post, percent): one-way ANOVA F(3, 381) = 3.12, p = 0.025, eta2 = 0.024; Tukey HSD F/CL more effective than F/VL, mean difference = 6.77%, SE = 2.25, p = 0.015, Cohen's d = 0.4. F/VL 4.82% [1.57, 8.09] vs F/CL 11.6% [8.11, 15.09]. Post-training levels 2.71 vs 2.81 (pairwise not significant).

outcomes.name: Post-training AUT fluency (number of uses)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of uses per AUT item, averaged over the two post-training items.

contrasts.reported: Mixed ANOVA on AUT number of responses: time F(1, 381) = 0.04, p = 0.90, eta2 = 0.0; time x condition F(3, 381) = 1.53, p = 0.2, eta2 = 0.01. Arm means shown only in Figure 4.

outcomes.name: GPT-4 creativity score of training stories (rounds 1-5)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4 prompted as a creative writing expert rates each story 1-5 for creativity; each story rated five times and averaged. Analyzed by condition x round mixed ANOVA and within-condition repeated-measures ANOVA. Feedback arrives only after each story, so round 1 is written before any AI feedback.

contrasts.reported: Condition x round mixed ANOVA: condition F(3, 381) = 29.48, p < 0.001, eta2 = 0.155; round F(4, 1524) = 10.21, p < 0.001, eta2 = 0.026; interaction F(12, 1524) = 2.01, p = 0.02, eta2 = 0.016. F/CL round 1 M = 3.03 (SD 0.66), round 3 M = 3.49 (SD 0.69), round 5 M = 3.44 (SD 0.75); F/VL round 1 M = 2.7 (SD 0.6), round 3 M = 2.98 (SD 0.79). NF conditions: no significant change across rounds (all p's > 0.05); their means are not printed. No pairwise between-condition comparison or arm means by condition are reported, so the direction of the condition effect is not stated.

company_involvement.description: Authors are at Technion; no external funding and no conflicts declared. GPT-4 is used through the OpenAI API but OpenAI has no stated role.
company_involvement.locator: p. 25, Funding and Conflicts of Interest

eligibility.reason: Conditions were filled by four separate recruitment batches, one per condition (p. 6, Section 2.1; p. 23, Section 4.5), and the paper never states random assignment, so people were compared under non-random assignment (quasi_people). Sample size (385 analyzed) and an output-scored outcome (OCSAI-scored AUT originality) are met. The AI is a GPT-4 coach that gives feedback and adjusts difficulty; the main AUT outcome is produced after AI is removed (after_ai).

one_line_finding: AUT originality rose from pre to post training in all four batch-assigned conditions (overall 2.6 to 2.81, F(1, 381) = 108.76), with no significant post-training difference between the AI-feedback arms and the no-AI NF/CL arm and a smaller gain for F/VL than F/CL (6.77 points, SE 2.25, p = 0.015) and lower post score than NF/VL (deltaM = 0.175, SE = 0.06, d = 0.41) (pp. 13-14, Section 3.2.1).
open_questions: Is assignment by recruitment batch (one batch per condition) treated as non-random? The paper calls it a between-subject design and refers to 'their assigned study condition' (p. 10) but never says random.
Is GPT-4 feedback on the participant's own story, with no content supplied, within scope as 'generative-AI assistance' for the with_ai question, or only as a coach in after_ai training?
GPT-4 story scores differ by condition already in round 1, before any feedback (F/VL 2.7 vs F/CL 3.03), consistent with batch differences.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output or do not bear on the three questions: self-reported story creativity per round (self_report; p. 16), perceived difficulty and fatigue (validation, pp. 10-11), suggestion usefulness ratings (Figure 7), and the animal semantic fluency control task (time F(1, 381) = 0.40, p = 0.52; interaction F(3, 381) = 0.29, p = 0.83; condition F(3, 381) = 5.0, p = 0.01; pp. 15, Figure 5). Printed statistics with apparent internal inconsistencies: F/VL pre-post t(96) = 2.75 reported with p < 0.001 (p. 13); post-training F(3, 381) = 3.34 reported with p = 0.002 (p. 13); fatigue interaction F(12, 1524) = 1.37, p = 0.017 called non-significant (p. 11); p. 6 says chi-squared tests found no age differences across groups, p. 23 reports a marginally significant age difference (p = 0.05). Table 1 sex counts do not sum to N for F/VL (41/55 = 96 of 97) or NF/CL (39/57 = 96 of 97). No standard deviation of the between-arm difference at participant level is given beyond arm means and SDs; the paper's F/VL vs NF/VL d = 0.41 is from Tukey HSD on post scores.
